EvoGroup: A Self-Evolving Harness for Group Agents in Shared Contexts

Xinyi Xu Affiliation: Sun Yat-sen University Email: xuxy299@mail2.sysu.edu.cn    Xiaoyang Li Affiliation: Sun Yat-sen University    Yucheng Feng Affiliation: Sun Yat-sen University    Wenqing Chen ††thanks: Corresponding author. Affiliation: Sun Yat-sen University    Youliang Yuan Affiliation: Longcat Team, Meituan Inc.    Wei Shi Affiliation: Longcat Team, Meituan Inc.    Rongxiang Weng Affiliation: Longcat Team, Meituan Inc.    Zibin Zheng Affiliation: Sun Yat-sen University
Abstract

With the rise of Group Agent such as Claude Tag, agents increasingly serve as digital workers for long-term team collaboration. These agents operate over shared contexts that continuously accumulate through multi-user interactions. However, existing agent memory systems are mainly designed for individual users and struggle to capture group-level knowledge in shared contexts, including group relationships and collaboratively formed knowledge. Manual memory strategies further limit adaptation to diverse and evolving shared contexts. To this end, we propose EvoGroup (EvoG), a self-evolving harness for group agents that starts from a minimal six-tool cold start and adapts through interaction with shared context. EvoG uses confidence and task outcomes to select informative trajectories, while also eliciting self-reflections on uncertainty in low-confidence cases. The analysis agent then examines selected trajectories through adaptive progressive disclosure, followed by bucketed analysis to synthesize high-level findings that guide the evolve agent in revising the Harness. Empirically, pass@1 on held-out split of EverMemBench improves from 71.07% to 89.58%, surpassing both self-evolving memory and human-designed harnesses, including Claude Code (85.83%). To evaluate generalization, we freeze the evolved harness and evaluate it on the unseen GroupMemBench, where, with GPT-5.5, it demonstrates effective generalization and outperforms both memory baselines and human-designed harnesses.11 1 The code for this manuscript is available at https://github.com/BigggFatttRabittt/EvoGroup.

1 Introduction

AI agents are gradually evolving from conversational assistants designed for individual users into digital workers that directly participate in multi-user interactions and team collaboration (OpenAI, 2026b; Spataro, 2025; Anthropic, 2026). In sustained multi-user collaboration, shared contexts continuously accumulate and evolve through interactions among multiple users. This makes memory essential for agents to accurately extract and apply relevant information from long-term conversations. A Group Agent must not only understand current messages but also integrate discussion topics, key events, member roles, and group decisions from prior interactions.

However, most existing agent memory systems are designed for single-user settings, organizing memory around individual experiences, preferences, and interaction histories (Park et al., 2023; Zhong et al., 2024; Packer et al., 2023). In group settings, information is distributed across multiple users, topics, and reply threads, and events may be supplemented or reinterpreted by different members. These characteristics make it difficult for existing memory systems to capture group dynamics and collaboratively formed knowledge (Yang et al., 2026a). In addition, existing memory systems typically predefine how memory is represented, updated, and retrieved (Chhikara et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026). For example, interaction histories may be stored in vector databases (Chhikara et al., 2025) or organized as knowledge graphs (Anokhin et al., 2024), with fixed mechanisms for updating outdated or conflicting information (Fang et al., 2026). When group structures, shared contexts, or task requirements change, adapting these systems often requires redesigning their memory storage or retrieval mechanisms. Such predefined designs limit the ability to adapt to different groups.

To address these challenges, we propose EvoGroup (EvoG), a self-evolving harness framework for Group Agent memory. EvoG starts from a minimal harness with only six tools and evolves through interaction. The evolution loop consists of four stages. (1) Interaction. The Group Agent uses the harness to answer queries over accumulated shared contexts, producing trajectories and confidence scores. For low-confidence queries, the agent additionally reflects on the reasons for its uncertainty before accessing the ground-truth. (2) Trajectory Selection. EvoG combines confidence with official evaluation to identify informative trajectories, including confident-incorrect, unconfident-correct, and unconfident-incorrect. (3) Analysis. The analysis agent uses Adaptive Progressive Disclosure (APD) to analyze selected trajectories, accessing trajectory details only when necessary. The agent also compresses detailed rationales into concise rationales. To identify recurring issues across trajectories, the agent performs bucketed analysis by grouping rationales according to inferred query semantics and further aggregating them into high-level findings. (4) Revision. Finally, the evolve agent uses analysis outputs to revise the Harness, producing Ht+1H_{t+1} for the next round of interaction. Through this loop, EvoG enables the harness to continuously adapt to the group and shared context.

We conduct extensive experiments to evaluate the effectiveness of EvoG. After evolution, the pass@1 of DeepSeek-V4-Flash on held-out split of EverMemBench improves from 71.07% to 89.58%, outperforming the human-designed Harnesses Codex (82.62%) and Claude Code (85.83%), as well as the strongest self-evolving memory baseline (55.95%). Across two additional backbone models, EvoG consistently improves pass@1 by 15.36–16.19 pp. To evaluate generalization beyond the evolution distribution, we freeze the evolved harness and apply it to GroupMemBench without further adaptation, where it continues to outperform self-evolving memory baselines and Claude Code. We further conduct component and process-level ablations and analyze capability transitions, confidence, self-reflection, APD analysis, and harness revisions to better understand how EvoG evolves. Together with our findings and open-source release, we hope EvoG inspires future efforts toward more capable and adaptive Group Agents.

2 EvoGroup

In this section, we propose EvoGroup (EvoG), a self-evolving harness loop for Group Agent Memory over shared contexts, as illustrated in Figure 2.

2.1 Interaction over Shared Contexts

In multi-user shared contexts, fixed memory organization and strategies struggle to adapt to evolving group information and task requirements. To address this limitation, EvoGroup enables self-evolution by treating the harness itself as the object of evolution.

Specifically, EvoGroup starts from a minimal modular harness H0H_{0}. The initial harness is equipped with only six basic tools: list_files, read_file, grep_search, write_file, query_records and create_file. From this cold start, EvoGroup repeatedly cycles through four stages: interaction, trajectory selection, analysis, and revision, allowing the harness to progressively accumulate memories and skills from interaction experience and thereby producing a sequence of increasingly capable harnesses:

H0,H1,…,HT.H_{0},H_{1},\ldots,H_{T}. (1)

At iteration tt, the Group Agent interacts with a shared group context and solves tasks using the current harness HtH_{t}. For a query qiq_{i}, the interaction produces an answer aia_{i} and a trajectory

τi=(qi,oi1,ui1,…,oiLi,uiLi,ai),\tau_{i}=\bigl(q_{i},o_{i}^{1},u_{i}^{1},\ldots,o_{i}^{L_{i}},u_{i}^{L_{i}},a_{i}\bigr), (2)

where oiℓo_{i}^{\ell} denotes the information observed at step ℓ\ell and uiℓu_{i}^{\ell} denotes the corresponding reasoning, communication, or tool-use action. The trajectory therefore records not only the final response, but also the intermediate decisions through which the Group Agent uses the components of HtH_{t}.

Along with its answer, the Group Agent reports a subjective confidence score ci∈[0,1]c_{i}\in[0,1]. We use a threshold γ\gamma (set to 0.50.5 in Figure 2) to distinguish confident from unconfident responses. If ci≤γc_{i}\leq\gamma, EvoGroup asks the Group Agent to revisit its reasoning and explain the source of its uncertainty. This self-reflection is generated before any supervision is revealed: neither the ground-truth answer nor the official evaluation result is provided to the agent. Consequently, the reflection captures the agent’s own diagnosis.

2.2 Confidence-Guided Trajectory Selection

During continuous interaction, different trajectories provide different evolutionary signals for self-evolution. We therefore combine the Agent’s confidence with official evaluation results to select informative trajectories.

After the interaction, an official evaluator supplies an external correctness signal yi∈{0,1}y_{i}\in\{0,1\} for the answer aia_{i}. Combining yiy_{i} with the confidence indicator zi=𝟏[ci>γ]z_{i}=\mathbf{1}[c_{i}>\gamma] partitions the collected trajectories into four groups:

𝒟CC\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{CC}} ={τi∣zi=1,yi=1},\displaystyle=\{\tau_{i}\mid z_{i}=1,\;y_{i}=1\}, (3)
𝒟CW\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{CW}} ={τi∣zi=1,yi=0},\displaystyle=\{\tau_{i}\mid z_{i}=1,\;y_{i}=0\},
𝒟UC\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{UC}} ={τi∣zi=0,yi=1},\displaystyle=\{\tau_{i}\mid z_{i}=0,\;y_{i}=1\},
𝒟UW\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{UW}} ={τi∣zi=0,yi=0}.\displaystyle=\{\tau_{i}\mid z_{i}=0,\;y_{i}=0\}.

The confident-and-correct subset 𝒟CC\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{CC}} represents routine successful behavior and is not prioritized for diagnosis. EvoGroup instead selects

𝒟sel=𝒟CW∪𝒟UC∪𝒟UW,\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{sel}}=\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{CW}}\cup\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{UC}}\cup\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{UW}}, (4)

which covers three complementary signals. Confident but incorrect trajectories reveal undetected reasoning failures or answer biases; unconfident but correct trajectories indicate fragile successes; and unconfident and incorrect trajectories capture failures that the Group Agent can partially recognize.

2.3 Trajectory Analysis

Agent trajectories contain numerous tool calls, observations, and shared-context details, making it difficult to locate the evidence responsible for a failure. EvoGroup addresses this challenge at two levels: it first uses Adaptive Progressive Disclosure (APD) to inspect and attribute individual trajectories on demand, and then uses bucketed analysis to aggregate recurring issues across trajectories into high-level findings.

APD Analysis. Rather than loading an entire, potentially long interaction into context at once, APD initially keeps the full trajectory hidden and exposes only a compact structural view. The Analysis Agent first locates a potentially problematic stage and then jumps to the corresponding local segment, requesting additional observations, actions, tool results, or communication records only when needed. This on-demand access focuses the analysis on diagnostically relevant evidence while reducing distraction from unrelated parts of the trajectory.

For each τi∈𝒟sel\tau_{i}\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{sel}}, the Analysis Agent identifies the stage at which the behavior deviates from a reliable solution process, attributes the observed failure or uncertainty to its most likely cause, and produces a detailed rationale ridetr_{i}^{\mathrm{det}}. EvoGroup then compresses the detailed diagnosis into a condensed rationale:

ricon=Compress⁡(ridet),r_{i}^{\mathrm{con}}=\operatorname{Compress}\!\left(r_{i}^{\mathrm{det}}\right), (5)

which retains the failure location, attributed cause, and actionable implication while removing instance-specific details that are unnecessary for cross-trajectory comparison.

Bucketed Analysis. To discover recurring issues beyond individual cases, EvoGroup organizes condensed rationales according to the semantic types of their queries. These types are not predefined. Instead, the Analysis Agent infers a type label gig_{i} from each query, for example, user profiling or temporal reasoning, and assigns analyses with the same inferred type to a shared bucket:

ℬg={ricon∣gi=g}.\mathcal{B}_{g}=\{r_{i}^{\mathrm{con}}\mid g_{i}=g\}. (6)

The Analysis Agent first analyzes evidence within each bucket to identify type-specific issues, and then compares the resulting issues across buckets to derive high-level findings. The resulting condensed rationales and high-level findings FtF_{t} summarize recurring sources of error and brittle success in the current Harness, and provide actionable evidence for subsequent harness revision.

2.4 Harness Revision

To enable more comprehensive and effective harness revision, we organize updates into four complementary interfaces: representation, operation, intervention, and policy, each targeting a distinct aspect of harness behavior to support continuous self-evolution from interaction.

Representation. This interface modifies how information is represented, organized, and linked within the Harness, without changing selection strategies. Updates include restructuring memory units, entity relations, working memory, and the context provided to the underlying model. Operation. This interface adds or modifies executable capabilities and their implementations, such as introducing query tools or revising retrieval algorithms. It determines what the harness can execute and how each operation is implemented. Intervention. This interface introduces checks, transformations, or constraints at execution boundaries, such as validating tool arguments before calls, normalizing returned results, and verifying outputs before returning them as final answers. Policy. This interface modifies the rules governing operation selection, timing, and ordering. Updates include adjusting prompts, skill invocation rules, retrieval parameters, search strategies, and operation composition and scheduling. Based on this distinction, the Evolve Agent selects the interface or interfaces that directly address each diagnosed issue.

3 Experiments

3.1 Setup

Benchmark & Baseline Methods. We use multi-party conversation benchmarks to evaluate the memory capabilities of group-chat agents. EverMemBench (Hu et al., 2026) is divided using stratified sampling, with 30% used as the held-in set for harness evolution and the remaining 70% used as the held-out set for evaluating the evolved harness. To evaluate cross-benchmark transfer, we then freeze the evolved harness and evaluate it on GroupMemBench (Yang et al., 2026b). We compare EvoGroup with structured-memory and self-evolving memory baselines, as well as human-designed agent Harnesses, including (1) FullContext, (2) Mem0 (Chhikara et al., 2025), (3) MemOS (Kang et al., 2025), (4) A-MEM (Xu et al., 2025), (5) MemRL (Zhang et al., 2026b), (6) Codex (OpenAI, 2025), and (7) Claude Code (Anthropic, 2025).

Models. For the evolution iterations and frozen transfer experiments (Sections 3.2, the Group Agent, Analysis Agent, and Evolve Agent use the same base model within each run. We evaluate three model configurations: GPT-5.5 (OpenAI, 2026a) with the non-thinking reasoning setting, DeepSeek-V4-Flash (DeepSeek-AI, 2026), and GLM-5.1 (GLM-5 Team et al., 2026).

Metric. We evaluate task effectiveness using pass@1. Each task is attempted once per evaluation run and is considered successful if it passes the official verifier. The final score is the proportion of successfully completed tasks. Trials terminated by system-level failures, such as timeouts, crashes, or missing outputs, are counted as unsuccessful. Detailed experimental settings are provided in Appendix .

3.2 Main Results

As shown in Table 1, we evaluate EvoGroup on GPT-5.5, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and GLM-5.1. After six self-evolution iterations, EvoGroup identifies the best-performing harness configuration, denoted by H∗H_{*}. On the held-out dataset, compared with the initial configuration H0H_{0}, H∗H_{*} improves the average pass rate by 16.2, 18.5, and 15.4 pp on the three models, respectively, demonstrating EvoGroup’s ability to consistently discover substantially better configurations. Meanwhile, EvoGroup outperforms the Structured Memory and Self-Evolving Memory baselines, as well as Claude Code and Codex, across all three backbones, except that its performance on GPT-5.5 is slightly below both Codex and Claude Code. However, since the evolution process is not limited to the number of iterations evaluated in our experiments, further iterations may yield additional performance gains. These results demonstrate that EvoGroup consistently discovers substantially stronger memory harness configurations across LLM backbones with different capabilities.

Generalization beyond the evolution benchmark. To evaluate whether the evolved harness generalizes beyond the distribution used for evolution, we freeze the harness evolved on EverMemBench and directly evaluate it on the unseen GroupMemBench without further adaptation. As shown in Table 4, on GPT-5.5, the evolved harness achieves the highest average pass rate of 63.89%, outperforming the initial harness by 2.01 points and the strongest human-designed harness by 8.46 points. On DeepSeek-V4-Flash, it achieves 71.14%, remaining within 2.95 points of the initial harness and 5.37 points of Codex, while outperforming the strongest memory baseline by 28.46 points. These results show that EvoG can transfer to an unseen benchmark while maintaining strong performance, although some performance degradation is observed with DeepSeek-V4-Flash.

3.3 Ablation Study

Component-level ablations. We evaluate the contribution of each harness component by replacing one component of the initial harness with its counterpart from the fully evolved harness, while keeping all other components unchanged. We consider Prompt, Tools, Middleware, Memory, and Skills separately. As shown in Figure 3, Tools and Prompt provide the largest gains, improving accuracy by 10.90 and 7.41 pp, respectively. Middleware, Memory, and Skills yield smaller gains of 1.27, 1.47, and 0.86 points. Using all evolved components achieves 89.58% accuracy, an 18.51 pp improvement over the initial harness at 71.07%. These results show that EvoGroup improves the harness through multiple components rather than prompt optimization alone.

Process-level ablations. We further examine three mechanisms in the self-evolution loop using DeepSeek-V4-Flash. All variants use the same cold-start harness configuration, evolution set, and token budget. As shown in Figure 4, removing trajectory selection increases Pass@1 from 73.33% to 74.86%, with a peak of 75.69%. Thus, analyzing all trajectories can support self-evolution, but requires more analysis time and greater token consumption.

Replacing APD with full-trace analysis yields a final Pass@1 of 69.44%, below its initial score. This suggests that, in shared-context task settings, directly analyzing complete trajectories may introduce irrelevant information and noise, whereas APD enables the Analysis Agent to focus on diagnostically relevant evidence and produce more effective evolution signals.

Removing bucketed analysis produces the lowest final Pass@1 of 67.08%. Without cross-trajectory aggregation, individual diagnoses may miss recurring failure patterns, resulting in more instance-specific and less reliable harness updates.

3.4 Analysis of Capability Transition

To examine how model capabilities evolve during self-evolution, we analyze task-level transitions between consecutive evolution rounds. As shown in Table 2, EvoGroup generally acquires new capabilities while retaining existing ones, although capability stability varies across models and evolution rounds. DeepSeek-V4-Flash maintains a retention rate above 91%, with regression rates ranging from 5.40% to 8.36%. GPT-5.5 also exhibits stable capability retention, with retention rates ranging from 92.5% to 94.3% and regression rates ranging from 5.7% to 7.5%. These results demonstrate that EvoGroup can improve task-solving capabilities across different LLM backbones while preserving most existing capabilities and maintaining relatively low regression rates throughout the evolution process.

3.5 Analysis of Confidence and Bias

We examine whether self-evolution improves both task performance and agent confidence by grouping trajectories into the four types defined in Section 2.2. As shown in Figure 7, for DeepSeek-V4-Flash, the proportion of confident-and-correct (CC) trajectories increases by 15.83%, while that of confident-but-wrong (CW) trajectories decreases by 6.25 %, indicating improvements in both task performance and confidence calibration, despite some fluctuations across intermediate iterations. For GPT-5.5, the proportion of CC trajectories increases by 10.62%, while that of CW trajectories decreases by 6.04%. Likewise, this shift indicates improved task performance and a more favorable confidence–correctness distribution. Overall, both models exhibit a higher proportion of confident-and-correct trajectories and a lower proportion of confident-but-incorrect trajectories after self-evolution.

3.6 Analysis of Self-reflection

To assess the agreement between self-reflection and trajectory-based diagnosis, we adopt three measures: localization-agreement, cause attribution-agreement, and diagnostic-evidence consistency. Localization-agreement reaches 84.0% for DeepSeek-V4-Flash and 74.4% for GPT-5.5, suggesting that self-reflection can often identify where a problem likely occurs without examining the full trajectory. In contrast, cause attribution-agreement is 49.2% and 62.0% for the two models, while diagnostic-evidence consistency is only 7.1% and 16.8%, respectively. These results indicate that self-reflection can provide a valuable yet not fully reliable localization signal before the full trajectory is read, directing the Analysis Agent toward likely problem regions and offering a more efficient, token-saving diagnostic pathway for harness self-evolution. Nevertheless, accurately verifying the root cause with sufficient evidence still relies on full trajectory analysis. Further improving the agent’s autonomous error-localization ability could reduce this reliance and further accelerate the harness self-evolution loop.

3.7 Analysis of Adaptive Progressive Disclosure

We compare Adaptive Progressive Disclosure (APD) with Full Trace Analysis while keeping the analysis model, budget, concurrency, and input content fixed. As shown in Table 3, APD reduces analysis time by 42.5% and token consumption by 41.5% on average across the 5 iterations. Most of the reduction comes from fewer input tokens, while output length remains similar. This shows that APD improves analysis efficiency by selectively accessing relevant trajectory segments instead of processing the full trace.

3.8 Effectiveness of Bucketed Analysis

Table 5 evaluates whether bucketed analysis produces useful evolution signals. Across self-evolution iterations, DeepSeek-V4-Flash achieves finding correctness rates of 71.40%-100.00%, adoption rates of 57.10%-66.70%, and repair rates of 41.40%-59.40%. GPT-5.5 maintains a finding correctness rate of 100.00%, with adoption rates of 50.00%-87.50% and repair rates of 33.30%-68.60%. These results show that bucketed analysis can distill recurring task-level failures into high-level findings that guide the Evolve Agent’s actions, although the resulting updates may still introduce regressions.

3.9 Analysis of Interface Importance

As shown in Figure 6, we analyze the use of the four revision interfaces by the Evolve Agent across evolution iterations. Policy accounts for the largest share of revisions, at 50.00% for DeepSeek-V4-Flash and 46.15% for GPT-5.5, followed by Representation. This may be because many problems encountered by group agents operating in shared contexts involve information retrieval and organization, as well as contextual dependencies across interactions. Both models use Intervention relatively infrequently, possibly because many problems can be addressed by adjusting policies or information representations without introducing additional runtime checks or constraints. Overall, EvoGroup primarily evolves through Policy and Representation updates, while modifications to executable capabilities and execution-boundary controls are more targeted. GPT-5.5 adopts a more conservative approach to self-evolution, whereas DeepSeek-V4-Flash makes more aggressive changes.

4 Related Work

Agent Memory. Agent memory aims to store and retrieve interaction information to support subsequent tasks (Park et al., 2023; Packer et al., 2023; Zhong et al., 2024). Existing methods typically organize memory using predefined structures (e.g., trees or graphs), combined with mechanisms such as profiling, reflection, and semantic compression (Park et al., 2023; Shinn et al., 2023; Packer et al., 2023; Chhikara et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025; Fang et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026). However, their memory storage and retrieval mechanisms are relatively fixed, making it difficult to adapt memory management to task requirements. Recent work has begun exploring self-evolving memory by optimizing memory operations through reinforcement learning or improving memory construction and updating (Yan et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026). However, these methods primarily target single-user. Hu et al. (2026); Yang et al. (2026b) have begun to investigate group-chat memory and its evaluation. Unlike single-user memory, group-chat memory must integrate information distributed across speakers, sessions, and temporal states while preserving user attribution, entity relationships, and contextual dependencies. To overcome the limitations of single-user designs and fixed memory paradigms, we propose EvoG, which enables memory mechanisms to evolve continuously based on interaction feedback.

Agent harness. An agent harness is a framework that organizes memory, planning, tools, and action policies around a foundation model to support agent-environment interaction. (Tang et al., 2026). Existing studies adapt harnesses through self-improvement, programmatic optimization, trajectory analysis, and code generation to improve task performance and adaptability (Lin et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026; Zhou, 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a; Ning et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026; Banu, 2026). However, most target coding, lacking efficient diagnostics for long interaction trajectories. In multi-user shared contexts, evidence scattered across speakers, sessions, and temporal states creates lengthy, interconnected trajectories, making full-trace analysis costly and prone to irrelevant information. To address this challenge, we propose EvoGroup.

5 Conclusion

In this work, we introduce EvoGroup, a self-evolving harness for group agent memory. By treating the harness as an evolvable system and learning evolution signals in the shared context, EvoGroup enables Group Agents to autonomously adapt to diverse groups. Result demonstrates that EvoGroup improves efficiency while maintaining strong performance. In the future, we will explore more realistic collaborative scenarios with diverse and long-term multi-user.

Appendix A Additional Experimental Results

A.1 Efficiency Analysis

Metric definitions. We separate online per-question cost from one-time preparation. Online metrics are Tokens per Question (Tok.), Tool Calls per Question (Calls), and Question Runtime (QA), each averaged over completed trials, including both correct and incorrect answers. Trials that terminate because of a system-level failure, timeout, crash, exception, or missing output are excluded from all three averages. Tok. is the sum of uncached input tokens, cached input tokens, and output tokens attributed to a question across all model calls. Each independently issued executable tool request counts as one call, and parallel requests are counted individually. Requests made by sub-agents are attributed to the parent question. Creating a sub-agent does not itself count as a tool request. QA time is the elapsed wall-clock time from the start of the question until completion and termination. Cold-Start Time (Cold) is a separate one-time preparation cost before answering. A dash denotes an unavailable or inapplicable measurement, not zero cost.

Cost profiles. Tables 6 and  show that EvoGroup keeps its per-question token cost within a relatively narrow range of 111K–200K, whereas Codex and Claude Code range from 66K to 668K. H∗H_{*} uses fewer tokens than Codex in all four settings, with reductions ranging from 0.8% to 81.6%, and uses fewer tokens than Claude Code in three of the four settings. The only exception is EverMemBench with DeepSeek-V4-Flash, where Claude Code uses 66K tokens per question compared with 123K for H∗H_{*}. Evolution also reduces the number of tool calls on EverMemBench from 14.28 to 12.87 with GPT-5.5 and from 16.47 to 12.57 with DeepSeek-V4-Flash. With DeepSeek-V4-Flash, H∗H_{*} makes fewer tool calls than either human-designed harness on both benchmarks, including 13.45 calls compared with Codex’s 27.59 on GroupMemBench. Overall, EvoGroup maintains relatively stable per-question token and tool-call costs while avoiding the large cost variation observed across the human-designed harnesses.

Runtime profiles. Tables 6 and  report the per-question answering time and cold-start overhead in seconds. Compared with Codex and Claude Code, H∗H_{*} reduces question runtime by 60.1%60.1\%–83.3%83.3\% and 77.4%77.4\%–85.9%85.9\%, respectively. On EverMemBench, evolution further reduces the answering time from 23.3623.36 s to 18.4418.44 s with GPT-5.5 and from 16.6716.67 s to 14.8214.82 s with DeepSeek-V4-Flash. Memory methods answer each question in 2.132.13–8.698.69 s, but their cold-start time ranges from 1,2411{,}241 s to 158,456158{,}456 s. In contrast, the cold-start time of H∗H_{*} is only 0.0740.074–0.1810.181 s. Evolution reduces the cold-start time relative to H0H_{0} in all four settings, including a reduction from 0.5890.589 s to 0.1810.181 s on EverMemBench with GPT-5.5. Overall, EvoGroup answers questions several times faster than the human-designed harnesses while keeping its cold-start time below one second.
